    <meta name="dc.description" content="Water stored in mountain snowpacks (i.e., snow water equivalent, SWE) represents an important but poorly characterized component of the terrestrial water cycle. The Western United States snow reanalysis (WUS–SR) dataset is novel in its combination of spatial resolution (~500 m), spatial extent (31°–49° N; 102°–125° W), and temporal continuity (daily over 1985–2021). WUS–SR is generated using a Bayesian framework with model-based snow estimates updated through the assimilation of cloud-free Landsat fractional snow-covered area observations. Over the WUS, the peak SWE verification with independent in situ measurements show correlation coefficient, mean difference (MD), and root mean squared difference (RMSD) of 0.77, −0.15 m, and 0.28 m, respectively. The effects of forest cover and Landsat image availability on peak SWE are assessed. WUS–SR peak SWE is well correlated (ranging from 0.75 to 0.91) against independent lidar-derived SWE taken near April 1st, with MD &lt;0.15 m and RMSD &lt;0.38 m. The dataset is useful for characterizing WUS mountain snow storage, and ultimately for improving snow-derived water resources management."/>

                <div class="c-article-body">
                    <section aria-labelledby="Abs1" data-title="Abstract" lang="en"><div class="c-article-section" id="Abs1-section"><h2 class="c-article-section__title js-section-title js-c-reading-companion-sections-item" id="Abs1">Abstract</h2><div class="c-article-section__content" id="Abs1-content"><p>Water stored in mountain snowpacks (i.e., snow water equivalent, SWE) represents an important but poorly characterized component of the terrestrial water cycle. The Western United States snow reanalysis (WUS–SR) dataset is novel in its combination of spatial resolution (~500 m), spatial extent (31°–49° N; 102°–125° W), and temporal continuity (daily over 1985–2021). WUS–SR is generated using a Bayesian framework with model-based snow estimates updated through the assimilation of cloud-free Landsat fractional snow-covered area observations. Over the WUS, the peak SWE verification with independent <i>in situ</i> measurements show correlation coefficient, mean difference (MD), and root mean squared difference (RMSD) of 0.77, −0.15 m, and 0.28 m, respectively. The effects of forest cover and Landsat image availability on peak SWE are assessed. WUS–SR peak SWE is well correlated (ranging from 0.75 to 0.91) against independent lidar-derived SWE taken near April 1<sup>st</sup>, with MD <0.15 m and RMSD <0.38 m. The dataset is useful for characterizing WUS mountain snow storage, and ultimately for improving snow-derived water resources management.</p></div></div></section><section lang="en"><div class="c-article-section" id="Abs2-section"><div class="c-article-section__content" id="Abs2-content"><div class="c-article-table-container"><div class="c-article-table-border c-table-scroll-wrapper"><div class="c-table-scroll-wrapper__content" data-component-scroll-wrapper=""><table class="data last-table"><tbody><tr><td class="u-text-left "><p>Measurement(s)</p></td><td class="u-text-left "><p>snow water equivalent, snow depth, fractional snow covered area</p></td></tr><tr><td class="u-text-left "><p>Technology Type(s)</p></td><td class="u-text-left "><p>Bayesian snow reanalysis framework with assimilation of fractional snow covered area</p></td></tr><tr><td class="u-text-left "><p>Sample Characteristic - Location</p></td><td class="u-text-left "><p>Western United States</p></td></tr></tbody></table></div></div></div></div></div></section>

                        <div class="main-content">
                            <section data-title="Background & Summary"><div class="c-article-section" id="Sec1-section"><h2 class="c-article-section__title js-section-title js-c-reading-companion-sections-item" id="Sec1">Background & Summary</h2><div class="c-article-section__content" id="Sec1-content"><p>Water stored in seasonal snowpacks, typically expressed in the form of snow water equivalent (SWE), provides a key resource relevant to water supply, hydropower generation, agricultural irrigation, river navigation, and urban usage in many areas of the globe. In the Western U.S. (WUS) it is estimated that more than half of runoff comes from seasonal snowmelt<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 1" title="Sturm, M., Goldstein, M. A. & Parr, C. Water and life from snow: A trillion dollar science question. Water Resour. Res. 53, 3534–3544 (2017)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR1" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e425">1</a>,<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2" title="Li, D., Wrzesien, M. L., Durand, M., Adam, J. & Lettenmaier, D. P. How much runoff originates as snow in the western United States, and how will that change in the future? Geophys. Res. Lett. 44, 6163–6172 (2017)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR2" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e428">2</a></sup>. Knowledge of SWE and its space-time variability impacts food, water and energy security, the financial stability of hydropower utilities, and public safety<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" title="Huning, L. S. & AghaKouchak, A. Global snow drought hot spots and characteristics. Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. 117, 19753–19759 (2020)." href="#ref-CR3" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e432">3</a>,<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" title="Yan, H. et al. Evaluating next-generation intensity–duration–frequency curves for design flood estimates in the snow-dominated western United States. Hydrol. Process. 34, 1255–1268 (2020)." href="#ref-CR4" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e432_1">4</a>,<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 5" title="Hamilton, A. L., Characklis, G. W. & Reed, P. M. Managing Financial Risk Trade-Offs for Hydropower Generation Using Snowpack-Based Index Contracts. Water Resour. Res. 56, e2020WR027212 (2020)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR5" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e435">5</a></sup>.</p><p><i>In situ</i> SWE data, even in the WUS where it is arguably most readily collected operationally, remains extremely sparse. Moreover, snow exhibits significant spatial heterogeneity due to variability in snowfall, redistribution and ablation controlled by local meteorological conditions, landcover, forest cover, and other physiographic characteristics<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 6" title="Larson, K. M. et al. Can we measure snow depth with GPS receivers? Geophys. Res. Lett. 36, L17502 (2009)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR6" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e444">6</a></sup>, especially in mountainous regions with high terrain complexity. The <i>in situ</i> snow stations that do exist are typically located in forest clearings, mid-elevations and flat terrain that do not necessarily sample the underlying heterogeneity of SWE<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 7" title="Nolin, A. W. et al. New snow metrics for a warming world. Hydrol. Process. 35 (2021)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR7" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e451">7</a>,<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 8" title="Molotch, N. P. & Bales, R. C. SNOTEL representativeness in the Rio Grande headwaters on the basis of physiographics and remotely sensed snow cover persistence. Hydrol. Process. 20, 723–739 (2006)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR8" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e454">8</a></sup>. Hence, <i>in situ</i> networks tend to provide an incomplete picture of the spatial patterns of SWE and how point-scale SWE integrates to basin-scale water volumes.</p><p>Remotely-sensed (satellite or airborne) observations of snow provide the potential to sample spatially-distributed characteristics of snow. The historically available satellite-borne measurements most closely related to SWE use Passive Microwave (PM, e.g., AMSR-E, SSMI) measurements to infer SWE or snow depth. However, PM measurements are typically obtained at coarse resolutions (tens of kilometers and thus incapable of resolving finer scale heterogeneity) and are highly sensitive to snowpack stratigraphy and microstructure, wet snow, and forest coverage (introducing significant uncertainty and bias into SWE estimates<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 9" title="Andreadis, K. M. & Lettenmaier, D. P. Assimilating remotely sensed snow observations into a macroscale hydrology model. Adv. Water Resour. 29, 872–886 (2006)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR9" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e464">9</a></sup>). Recent and future airborne and spaceborne concepts aim to measure snow depth (from lidar<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 10" title="Markus, T. et al. The Ice, Cloud, and land Elevation Satellite-2 (ICESat-2): Science requirements, concept, and implementation. Remote Sens. Environ. 190, 260–273 (2017)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR10" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e468">10</a>,<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 11" title="Painter, T. H. et al. The Airborne Snow Observatory: Fusion of scanning lidar, imaging spectrometer, and physically-based modeling for mapping snow water equivalent and snow albedo. Remote Sens. Environ. 184, 139–152 (2016)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR11" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e471">11</a></sup>, photogrammetry, radar<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 12" title="Lievens, H. et al. Snow depth variability in the Northern Hemisphere mountains observed from space. Nat. Commun. 10, 4629 (2019)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR12" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e475">12</a></sup>), or SWE (from P-band<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 13" title="Yueh, S. et al. UAS-based P-band signals of opportunity for remote sensing of snow and root zone soil moisture. in Sensors, Systems, and Next-Generation Satellites XXII vol. 10785 107850B (International Society for Optics and Photonics, 2018)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR13" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e479">13</a></sup>, C-band, X-band<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 14" title="Shi, J. & Dozier, J. Estimation of snow water equivalence using SIR-C/X-SAR. II. Inferring snow depth and particle size. IEEE Trans. Geosci. Remote Sens. 38, 2475–2488 (2000)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR14" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e483">14</a></sup>, and Ku-band radar<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 15" title="Nghiem, S. V. & Tsai, W.-Y. Global snow cover monitoring with spaceborne K/sub u/-band scatterometer. IEEE Trans. Geosci. Remote Sens. 39, 2118–2134 (2001)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR15" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e488">15</a></sup>). These newer methods show promise but cannot yet provide a long-term spatially-distributed SWE record.</p><p>To leverage remotely-sensed and <i>in situ</i> datasets relevant to snow processes, data assimilation combined with snow and land surface models (LSMs) can be used to constrain model estimates based on snow related observations. Global reanalysis products including ERA5<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 16" title="Hersbach, H. et al. The ERA5 global reanalysis. Q. J. R. Meteorol. Soc. 146, 1999–2049 (2020)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR16" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e498">16</a></sup>, ERA5-land<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 17" title="Muñoz-Sabater, J. et al. ERA5-Land: a state-of-the-art global reanalysis dataset for land applications. Earth Syst. Sci. Data 13, 4349–4383 (2021)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR17" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e502">17</a></sup>, JRA55<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 18" title="Kobayashi, S. et al. The JRA-55 Reanalysis: General Specifications and Basic Characteristics. J. Meteorol. Soc. Jpn. Ser II 93, 5–48 (2015)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR18" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e506">18</a></sup>, GLDAS<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 19" title="Rodell, M. et al. The Global Land Data Assimilation System. Bull. Am. Meteorol. Soc. 85, 381–394 (2004)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR19" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e510">19</a></sup>, MERRA2<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 20" title="Gelaro, R. et al. The Modern-Era Retrospective Analysis for Research and Applications, Version 2 (MERRA-2). J. Clim. 30, 5419–5454 (2017)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR20" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e515">20</a></sup>, and GlobSnow v3.0<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 21" title="Luojus, K. et al. GlobSnow v3.0 Northern Hemisphere snow water equivalent dataset. Sci. Data 8, 163 (2021)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR21" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e519">21</a></sup> estimate terrestrial snow accumulation and melt with commonly used LSMs (e.g., VIC, SiB, Catchment, Noah) at scales of ~ 0.1° to 1°. Though coarse resolutions are typical in global applications, they do not provide the desired resolution to capture spatial variations, especially in complex terrain<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 22" title="Wrzesien, M. L., Pavelsky, T. M., Durand, M. T., Dozier, J. & Lundquist, J. D. Characterizing Biases in Mountain Snow Accumulation From Global Data Sets. Water Resour. Res. 55, 9873–9891 (2019)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR22" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e523">22</a></sup>. Additionally, several studies have found large uncertainties in SWE volumes derived from various input forcings and models applied over global snow covered mountains<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 23" title="Xu, Y., Jones, A. & Rhoades, A. A quantitative method to decompose SWE differences between regional climate models and reanalysis datasets. Sci. Rep. 9, 16520 (2019)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR23" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e527">23</a>,<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 24" title="Kim, R. S. et al. Snow Ensemble Uncertainty Project (SEUP): quantification of snow water equivalent uncertainty across North America via ensemble land surface modeling. The Cryosphere 15, 771–791 (2021)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR24" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e530">24</a></sup>. Snow-focused products over the U.S. using data assimilation include the Snow Data Assimilation System (SNODAS<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 25" title="National Operational Hydrologic Remote Sensing Center. Snow Data Assimilation System (SNODAS) Data Products at NSIDC, Version 1. (2004)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR25" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e534">25</a></sup>) product and the University of Arizona SWE dataset (UA<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 26" title="Zeng, X., Broxton, P. & Dawson, N. Snowpack Change From 1982 to 2016 Over Conterminous United States. Geophys. Res. Lett. 45, 12,940–12,947 (2018)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR26" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e538">26</a></sup>). SNODAS daily SWE estimates are available from 2004 at the spatial resolution of 1 km × 1 km. UA daily SWE estimates start from 1982 at the spatial resolution of 4 km × 4 km. Hence, SNODAS has a more limited temporal coverage (less than 20 years), and UA is at relatively coarse resolution that can be suboptimal for assessing spatial variability in mountainous domains. In the mountainous WUS, historical space–time continuous snow estimates at high to moderate resolution and with low uncertainty are needed.</p><p>To fill this gap, we use a Bayesian data assimilation approach that leverages high-resolution remotely-sensed visible and near infrared (Vis-NIR) measurements that provide information on fractional snow-covered area (fSCA) and how its seasonal evolution is related to SWE. Specifically, the approach yields a new snow reanalysis dataset across the WUS (Fig. <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="figure anchor" href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#Fig1">1</a>) over the Landsat–era (water years (WYs) 1985 to 2021). The dataset is publicly available at National Snow and Ice Data Center (10.5067/PP7T2GBI52I2)<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 27" title="Fang, Y., Liu, Y. & Margulis, S. Western United States UCLA Daily Snow Reanalysis. NASA Earth Data, 
                  https://doi.org/10.5067/PP7T2GBI52I2
                  
                 (2022)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR27" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e549">27</a></sup>. The daily snow reanalysis framework accounts for a priori uncertainties in meteorological forcings and other snow model parameters and reduces the uncertainty via a Bayesian data assimilation approach as described in more detail in the Methods section. The snow reanalysis SWE estimates are verified against independent <i>in situ</i> SWE measurements and lidar-based SWE products. Previous applications of the method over the Sierra Nevada have demonstrated the ability to characterize historical snow droughts, characterize snowfall estimates from SWE accumulation patterns, and improve streamflow predictions<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" title="Huning, L. S. & AghaKouchak, A. Approaching 80 years of snow water equivalent information by merging different data streams. Sci. Data 7, 333 (2020)." href="#ref-CR28" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e556">28</a>,<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" title="Margulis, S. A., Girotto, M., Cortés, G. & Durand, M. A Particle Batch Smoother Approach to Snow Water Equivalent Estimation. J. Hydrometeorol. 16, 1752–1772 (2015)." href="#ref-CR32" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e599">32</a>,<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" title="Margulis, S. A., Cortés, G., Girotto, M. & Durand, M. A Landsat-Era Sierra Nevada Snow Reanalysis (1985–2015). J. Hydrometeorol. 17, 1203–1221 (2016)." href="#ref-CR33" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e599_1">33</a>,<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 34" title="Margulis, S. A., Liu, Y. & Baldo, E. A Joint Landsat- and MODIS-Based Reanalysis Approach for Midlatitude Montane Seasonal Snow Characterization. Front. Earth Sci. 7, 272 (2019)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR34" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e602">34</a></sup> (Fig. <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="figure anchor" href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#Fig2">2</a>) is applied to generate a new Landsat-era dataset over the WUS, herein referred to as the Western U.S. – Snow Reanalysis (WUS–SR). The dataset contains space–time continuous SWE and fractional snow-covered area (fSCA) estimates constrained by remotely-sensed (Landsat) fSCA using a particle batch smoother (PBS) data assimilation technique.</p><div class="c-article-section__figure js-c-reading-companion-figures-item" data-test="figure" data-container-section="figure" id="figure-2" data-title="Fig. 2"><figure><figcaption><b id="Fig2" class="c-article-section__figure-caption" data-test="figure-caption-text">Fig. 2</b></figcaption><div class="c-article-section__figure-content"><div class="c-article-section__figure-item"><picture class="c-article-section__figure-picture"><source type="image/webp" srcset="//media.springernature.com/lw685/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41597-022-01768-7/MediaObjects/41597_2022_1768_Fig2_HTML.png?as=webp"><img aria-describedby="figure-2-desc" class="c-article-section__figure-description" data-test="bottom-caption" id="figure-2-desc"><p>Flowchart for the Bayesian snow reanalysis framework used to generate the WUS–SR dataset (adapted from Margulis <i>et al</i>.<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 34" title="Margulis, S. A., Liu, Y. & Baldo, E. A Joint Landsat- and MODIS-Based Reanalysis Approach for Midlatitude Montane Seasonal Snow Characterization. Front. Earth Sci. 7, 272 (2019)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR34" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e622">34</a></sup>).</p></div></div></figure></div><p>The snow reanalysis framework generates an ensemble of (equally likely) prior snow estimates using a land surface model (LSM) driven by meteorological forcing, topographic data and landcover data (red boxes in Fig. <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="figure anchor" href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#Fig2">2</a>). Uncertainty is expressed via perturbations related to precipitation (snowfall), the snow depletion curve and snow albedo in each ensemble member (described in the Uncertainty Parameters and Measurement Error section). The reanalysis step assimilates Landsat-derived fSCA measurements to provide posterior snow estimates (blue boxes in Fig. <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="figure anchor" href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#Fig2">2</a>). More specifically, the a priori (equal) weights are updated to posterior weights that reflect the likelihood that a given ensemble member fits the fSCA measurements<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 34" title="Margulis, S. A., Liu, Y. & Baldo, E. A Joint Landsat- and MODIS-Based Reanalysis Approach for Midlatitude Montane Seasonal Snow Characterization. Front. Earth Sci. 7, 272 (2019)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR34" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e643">34</a></sup>. The posterior weights, when combined with the prior ensemble estimates (e.g., SWE) can be used to derive posterior estimates (ensemble statistics) of the relevant states. The resulting posterior SWE, snow depth and fSCA make up the published dataset.</p><p>While the snow reanalysis framework could be applied with any LSMs and their static and dynamic model inputs, in creating the WUS–SR, we use the same setup as described in Margulis <i>et al</i>.<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 34" title="Margulis, S. A., Liu, Y. & Baldo, E. A Joint Landsat- and MODIS-Based Reanalysis Approach for Midlatitude Montane Seasonal Snow Characterization. Front. Earth Sci. 7, 272 (2019)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR34" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e653">34</a></sup>. In summary, a spatially-distributed version of the SSiB–SAST LSM<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" title="Sun, S. & Xue, Y. Implementing a new snow scheme in Simplified Simple Biosphere Model. Adv. Atmospheric Sci. 18, 335–354 (2001)." href="#ref-CR35" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e657">35</a>,<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" title="Xue, Y., Sun, S., Kahan, D. S. & Jiao, Y. Impact of parameterizations in snow physics and interface processes on the simulation of snow cover and runoff at several cold region sites. J. Geophys. Res. Atmospheres 108 (2003)." href="#ref-CR36" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e657_1">36</a>,<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 37" title="Sun, S., Jin, J. & Xue, Y. A simplified layer snow model for global and regional studies. J Geophys Res 104, 19587–19597 (1999)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR37" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e660">37</a></sup> using the BATS<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 38" title="Dickinson, R. E., Henderson-Sellers, A. & Kennedy, P. J. Biosphere-Atmosphere Transfer Scheme (BATS) version 1e as coupled to the NCAR community climate model. Technical note. [NCAR (National Center for Atmospheric Research)]. 
                  https://doi.org/10.5065/D67W6959
                  
                 (1993)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR38" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e664">38</a></sup> snow albedo model and coupled with the Liston<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 39" title="Liston, G. E. Representing Subgrid Snow Cover Heterogeneities in Regional and Global Models. J. Clim. 17, 1381–1397 (2004)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR39" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e668">39</a></sup> Snow Depletion Curve (SDC) model is used. The SSiB–SAST LSM models a three-layer snowpack when snow depth is above 5 cm, and uses a one-layer scheme when snow depth is below 5 cm. SWE at each layer is computed by mass balance with components including snowfall, rainfall, snowmelt, runoff and evaporation at the snow surface layer<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 36" title="Xue, Y., Sun, S., Kahan, D. S. & Jiao, Y. Impact of parameterizations in snow physics and interface processes on the simulation of snow cover and runoff at several cold region sites. J. Geophys. Res. Atmospheres 108 (2003)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR36" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e673">36</a></sup>. Snow density, and therefore snow depth, is determined by the SAST compaction process as described in Sun and Xue<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 35" title="Sun, S. & Xue, Y. Implementing a new snow scheme in Simplified Simple Biosphere Model. Adv. Atmospheric Sci. 18, 335–354 (2001)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR35" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e677">35</a></sup>. For computational reasons, a uniform spatial resolution of 16 arcseconds (~500 m) is chosen with hourly outputs aggregated to the daily time step using an ensemble of 50 members. The SDC provides the mechanism whereby modeled estimates of SWE (and its sub-grid heterogeneity) provide predicted estimates of fSCA. For the reanalysis, the LSM–SDC model is applied separately at each pixel to the bare snow and forest covered fractions. It is assumed that Landsat sensors cannot see snow under the forest canopy. Therefore, only the predicted fSCA over bare soil is compared to the Landsat fSCA measurements in the assimilation step for each grid, while the update is applied to both bare and forested pixel fractions to obtain the grid-averaged SWE<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 34" title="Margulis, S. A., Liu, Y. & Baldo, E. A Joint Landsat- and MODIS-Based Reanalysis Approach for Midlatitude Montane Seasonal Snow Characterization. Front. Earth Sci. 7, 272 (2019)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR34" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e681">34</a></sup>. The Bayesian update is applied in a batch over one WY at a time, where the batch of fSCA measurements from that year are used together to derive the posterior weights and estimates. Table <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="table anchor" href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#Tab1">1</a> summarizes the models and method used in the snow reanalysis framework.</p><div class="c-article-table" data-test="inline-table" data-container-section="table" id="table-2"><figure><figcaption class="c-article-table__figcaption"><b id="Tab1" data-test="table-caption">Table 1 Modules used in the snow reanalysis framework.</b></figcaption><div class="u-hide-print"><a class="c-article__pill-button" data-test="table-link" data-track="click" data-track-action="view table" data-track-label="button" rel="nofollow" href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7/tables/2" aria-label="Full size table 2"><span>Full size table</span><svg width="16" height="16" focusable="false" role="img" aria-hidden="true" class="u-icon"><use xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="#icon-eds-i-chevron-right-small"></use></svg></a></div></figure></div><h3 class="c-article__sub-heading" id="Sec4">Land surface model inputs</h3><p>To generate the WUS–SR dataset, globally-available datasets are used as inputs. This includes the MERRA2<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 20" title="Gelaro, R. et al. The Modern-Era Retrospective Analysis for Research and Applications, Version 2 (MERRA-2). J. Clim. 30, 5419–5454 (2017)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR20" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e787">20</a></sup> near-surface meteorological forcing data, 30-m Shuttle Radar Topography Mission (SRTM<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 40" title="Farr, T. G. et al. The Shuttle Radar Topography Mission. Rev. Geophys. 45 (2007)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR40" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e791">40</a>,<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 41" title="NASA. Shuttle Radar Topography Mission (SRTM). 
                  https://www2.jpl.nasa.gov/srtm/
                  
                 (2013)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR41" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e794">41</a></sup>) digital elevation model (DEM) for topographic data (with gaps filled by the Advanced Spaceborne Thermal Emission and Reflection, ASTER<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 42" title="NASA. ASTER. 
                  http://asterweb.jpl.nasa.gov/
                  
                 (2001)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR42" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e798">42</a></sup>, version 2), 1-km Advanced Very High Resolution Radiometer (AVHRR<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 43" title="Hansen, M. C., Defries, R. S., Townshend, J. R. G. & Sohlberg, R. Global land cover classification at 1 km spatial resolution using a classification tree approach. Int. J. Remote Sens. 21, 1331–1364 (2000)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR43" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e802">43</a>,<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 44" title="Advanced Very High Resolution Radiometer (AVHRR). U.S. Geological Survey 
                  https://doi.org/10.5066/F7K35S5K
                  
                 (2017)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR44" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e805">44</a></sup>) landcover data and 30-m Global Land Cover Facility (recently updated to the Landsat Tree Canopy Version 4, TCC<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 45" title="Sexton, J. O. et al. Global, 30-m resolution continuous fields of tree cover: Landsat-based rescaling of MODIS vegetation continuous fields with lidar-based estimates of error. Int. J. Digit. Earth 6, 427–448 (2013)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR45" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e809">45</a>,<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 46" title="Sexton, J. O. et al. Global 30m Landsat Tree Canopy Version 4. 
                  https://e4ftl01.cr.usgs.gov/MEASURES/GFCC30TC.003/
                  
                ." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR46" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e812">46</a></sup>) forest cover fraction data. The TCC data is available in 2000, 2005, 2010, and 2015 where each timestamped year represents multi-year average forest cover conditions during that period. Rather than implementing time-varying forest cover, the time-averaged forest cover over these 4 composites is applied for the whole reanalysis period. All inputs are downscaled or aggregated to the chosen model resolution. For example, the 1-km AVHRR dataset is first interpolated to the 30-m resolution of the raw SRTM DEM at the nearest grid and then aggregated to the 480-m model resolution.</p><p>The meteorological forcings used in this dataset include 2-m air temperature, 2-m specific humidity, 10-m zonal and meridional wind speed, surface pressure, surface precipitation, and surface downwelling shortwave<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 34" title="Margulis, S. A., Liu, Y. & Baldo, E. A Joint Landsat- and MODIS-Based Reanalysis Approach for Midlatitude Montane Seasonal Snow Characterization. Front. Earth Sci. 7, 272 (2019)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR34" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e819">34</a></sup>. The raw MERRA2 precipitation is perturbed to account for the expected bias and uncertainty in snowfall inputs (see more detail in the Uncertainty Parameters and Measurement Error section). In addition to precipitation, the bias and uncertainties of MERRA2 air temperature, dew point temperature (computed from MERRA2 specific humidity), and shortwave radiation are represented via ensemble perturbations. Hourly snowfall is computed by downscaled and bias-corrected air temperature and precipitation using a rain–snow threshold of 2 °C. When air temperature is below the threshold, precipitation is classified as snowfall. Table <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="table anchor" href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#Tab2">2</a> summarizes the static and dynamic inputs used to generate the dataset, as well as assimilated data described in the next section.</p><div class="c-article-table" data-test="inline-table" data-container-section="table" id="table-3"><figure><figcaption class="c-article-table__figcaption"><b id="Tab2" data-test="table-caption">Table 2 Static and dynamic model inputs and assimilated data.</b></figcaption><div class="u-hide-print"><a class="c-article__pill-button" data-test="table-link" data-track="click" data-track-action="view table" data-track-label="button" rel="nofollow" href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7/tables/3" aria-label="Full size table 3"><span>Full size table</span><svg width="16" height="16" focusable="false" role="img" aria-hidden="true" class="u-icon"><use xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="#icon-eds-i-chevron-right-small"></use></svg></a></div></figure></div><h3 class="c-article__sub-heading" id="Sec5">Assimilated landsat fSCA data</h3><p>The timeseries of derived Landsat fSCA (raw resolution of ~30 m aggregated to 16 arcseconds), over the course of a WY is used as the measurement constraint in the Bayesian particle batch smoother (PBS) update. The retrieval of Landsat fSCA is obtained through applying linear spectral unmixing methods described in Painter <i>et al</i>.<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 47" title="Painter, T. H., Dozier, J., Roberts, D. A., Davis, R. E. & Green, R. O. Retrieval of subpixel snow-covered area and grain size from imaging spectrometer data. Remote Sens. Environ. 85, 64–77 (2003)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR47" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e1012">47</a></sup> and Cortés <i>et al</i>.<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 48" title="Cortés, G., Girotto, M. & Margulis, S. A. Analysis of sub-pixel snow and ice extent over the extratropical Andes using spectral unmixing of historical Landsat imagery. Remote Sens. Environ. 141, 64–78 (2014)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR48" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e1019">48</a></sup> using Vis-NIR reflectance measured from three Landsat satellites: 1) Landsat 5 Thematic Mapper (TM) from 1985 to 2011; 2) Landsat 7 enhanced Thematic Mapper (ETM+) from 1999 to present, and 3) Landsat 8 Operational Land Images (OLI) from 2013 to present. Orbital characteristics of the Landsat platform provide swath images every 16 days (~23 images per year). Adjacent swaths contain some overlap such that some locations may have up to ~46 fSCA images from a single satellite per year. This is the typical number of available measurements from WYs 1985–1999 (when only Landsat 5 is available) and in 2012 (when only Landsat 7 is available). In the other years, where two satellites are available (i.e., WYs 2000–2011 and 2013–present), the number of available measurements is doubled. The failure of Landsat 7 Scan Line Corrector (starting in 2003) removes ~22% of its image areas, thus reducing the number of measurements per year (USGS<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 49" title="USGS. SLC-off Gap-Filled Products Gap-Fill Algorithm Methodology. 
                  https://www.usgs.gov/media/files/landsat-7-slc-gap-filled-products-phase-two-methodology
                  
                 (2004)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR49" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e1023">49</a></sup>). However, the number of measurements described above provide only an upper limit on those used in the WUS–SR. Cloud contamination can significantly reduce the number of available (assimilated) measurements. Following the cloud screening methods described in Margulis <i>et al</i>.<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 34" title="Margulis, S. A., Liu, Y. & Baldo, E. A Joint Landsat- and MODIS-Based Reanalysis Approach for Midlatitude Montane Seasonal Snow Characterization. Front. Earth Sci. 7, 272 (2019)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR34" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e1031">34</a></sup> and Liu <i>et al</i>.<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 50" title="Liu, Y., Fang, Y. & Margulis, S. A. Spatiotemporal distribution of seasonal snow water equivalent in High Mountain Asia from an 18-year Landsat–MODIS era snow reanalysis dataset. The Cryosphere 15, 5261–5280 (2021)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR50" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e1038">50</a></sup>, the internal Landsat cloud mask is used to attempt to exclude images with cloud cover fraction greater than 40%. For those images included, the internal cloud masks are used to screen out any cloudy pixels. Thus, areas identified as contaminated by clouds are removed before assimilation which reduces the available number of measurements. Though errors introduced by omission or commission are inevitable, they are implicitly accounted for in the snow reanalysis framework as described in the <i>Measurement Error</i> section below.</p><p>Figure <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="figure anchor" href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#Fig3">3</a> shows that the total numbers of cloud-free fSCA measurements are much fewer in WYs 1992 and 2012 when only one Landsat platform is available over 10 months of the WY compared to WYs 2002 and 2018 when two Landsat satellites are available over the full WY. The number of available fSCA measurements is associated with satellite swaths that may cause spatial artifacts in posterior estimates within a WY. Grid cells with no fSCA measurements (no assimilation) or limited fSCA measurements may yield inconsistent results with grid cells that have abundant fSCA measurements. In the PN, spatial artifacts in the SWE estimates are more frequently observed when only one Landsat is available, where cloudy days are more common in the melting season. The method is capable of jointly assimilating other fSCA data (e.g., MODIS<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 34" title="Margulis, S. A., Liu, Y. & Baldo, E. A Joint Landsat- and MODIS-Based Reanalysis Approach for Midlatitude Montane Seasonal Snow Characterization. Front. Earth Sci. 7, 272 (2019)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR34" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e1051">34</a></sup>) or other relevant snow data (e.g., snow depth<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 51" title="Margulis, S. A., Fang, Y., Li, D., Lettenmaier, D. P. & Andreadis, K. The Utility of Infrequent Snow Depth Images for Deriving Continuous Space-Time Estimates of Seasonal Snow Water Equivalent. Geophys. Res. Lett. 46, 5331–5340 (2019)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR51" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e1055">51</a></sup>). The dataset presented herein is chosen to use Landsat-only data to provide a long-term homogeneous snow reanalysis product.</p><div class="c-article-section__figure js-c-reading-companion-figures-item" data-test="figure" data-container-section="figure" id="figure-3" data-title="Fig. 3"><figure><figcaption><b id="Fig3" class="c-article-section__figure-caption" data-test="figure-caption-text">Fig. 3</b></figcaption><div class="c-article-section__figure-content"><div class="c-article-section__figure-item"><picture class="c-article-section__figure-picture"><source type="image/webp" srcset="//media.springernature.com/lw685/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41597-022-01768-7/MediaObjects/41597_2022_1768_Fig3_HTML.png?as=webp"><img aria-describedby="figure-3-desc" src="//media.springernature.com/lw685/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41597-022-01768-7/MediaObjects/41597_2022_1768_Fig3_HTML.png" alt="Fig. 3" loading="lazy" width="685" height="650"></picture><div class="c-article-section__figure-link"><a class="c-article__pill-button" data-test="article-link" data-track="click" data-track-label="button" data-track-action="view figure" href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7/figures/3" data-track-dest="link:Figure3 Full size image" aria-label="Full size image figure 3" rel="nofollow"><span>Full size image</span><svg width="16" height="16" focusable="false" role="img" aria-hidden="true" class="u-icon"><use xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="#icon-eds-i-chevron-right-small"></use></svg></a></div></div><div class="c-article-section__figure-description" data-test="bottom-caption" id="figure-3-desc"><p>Illustration of the number of cloud-free Landsat measurements used in the WUS–SR for four WYs (top four panels) and Landsat mission timelines (bottom panel). Landsat images with diagnosed cloud fractions of 40% are excluded entirely and those will less than 40% use the Landsat cloud mask to screen out cloudy measurements. The four illustrative WYs include: (<b>a</b>) WY 1992 and (<b>c</b>) 2012 when one Landsat satellite is in orbit, and (<b>b</b>) WY 2002 and (<b>d</b>) 2018 when two Landsat satellites are in orbit. The stripes showing a larger number of measurements are the overlapping areas between adjacent Landsat tiles. The temporal coverage of measurements in (<b>e</b>) shows the Landsat 5, 7 and 8 mission timelines. Periods with only one Landsat satellite are shaded with a gray background. The orange hatched areas indicate the four WYs present in maps in the top panels.</p></div></div></figure></div><h3 class="c-article__sub-heading" id="Sec6">Uncertainty parameters and measurement error</h3><p>The ensemble Bayesian framework described above is applied by considering and modeling key sources of uncertainty and error. These include uncertainty in meteorological inputs and model parameters controlling snow albedo and sub-grid distribution, and fSCA measurement errors as described in more detail below and which follow those in Margulis <i>et al</i>.<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 34" title="Margulis, S. A., Liu, Y. & Baldo, E. A Joint Landsat- and MODIS-Based Reanalysis Approach for Midlatitude Montane Seasonal Snow Characterization. Front. Earth Sci. 7, 272 (2019)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR34" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e1103">34</a></sup>.</p><h4 class="c-article__sub-heading c-article__sub-heading--small" id="Sec7">Perturbed meteorological forcings</h4><p>The a priori meteorological forcing uncertainties are embedded in the prior ensemble via perturbations to the nominal (MERRA2) inputs using parameters randomly generated from specified distributions. The uncertainty and bias correction models used are similar to those that have been successfully applied to the Sierra Nevada<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 33" title="Margulis, S. A., Cortés, G., Girotto, M. & Durand, M. A Landsat-Era Sierra Nevada Snow Reanalysis (1985–2015). J. Hydrometeorol. 17, 1203–1221 (2016)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR33" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e1114">33</a></sup>, Andes<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 52" title="Cortés, G. & Margulis, S. Impacts of El Niño and La Niña on interannual snow accumulation in the Andes: Results from a high-resolution 31 year reanalysis. Geophys. Res. Lett. 44, 6859–6867 (2017)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR52" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e1118">52</a></sup>, and High Mountain Asia<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 50" title="Liu, Y., Fang, Y. & Margulis, S. A. Spatiotemporal distribution of seasonal snow water equivalent in High Mountain Asia from an 18-year Landsat–MODIS era snow reanalysis dataset. The Cryosphere 15, 5261–5280 (2021)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR50" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e1122">50</a></sup> to downscale and perturb forcings. Forcing downscaling uses a topographic correction approach following Girotto <i>et al</i>.<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 53" title="Girotto, M., Margulis, S. A. & Durand, M. Probabilistic SWE reanalysis as a generalization of deterministic SWE reconstruction techniques: PROBABILISTIC SWE REANALYSIS. Hydrol. Process. 28, 3875–3895 (2014)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR53" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e1129">53</a></sup>. The raw MERRA2 forcings are first (bilinearly) interpolated to the snow reanalysis grid followed by an elevation correction using differences between the (coarser resolution) MERRA2 and (higher resolution) reanalysis DEMs. Downscaled precipitation, air temperature, dew point temperature and shortwave inputs are bias-corrected and perturbed using the formulation<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 34" title="Margulis, S. A., Liu, Y. & Baldo, E. A Joint Landsat- and MODIS-Based Reanalysis Approach for Midlatitude Montane Seasonal Snow Characterization. Front. Earth Sci. 7, 272 (2019)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR34" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e1134">34</a></sup>:</p><div id="Equ1" class="c-article-equation"><div class="c-article-equation__content"><span class="mathjax-tex">$${PPT}_{j}={b}_{j}\cdot {PPT}_{MERRA{\rm{2}}}$$</span></div><div class="c-article-equation__number">
                    (1)
                </div></div><div id="Equ2" class="c-article-equation"><div class="c-article-equation__content"><span class="mathjax-tex">$${T}_{a,j}={T}_{a{\rm{,}}MERRA{\rm{2}}}{\rm{+}}{\varepsilon }_{{T}_{a,j}}$$</span></div><div class="c-article-equation__number">
                    (2)
                </div></div><div id="Equ3" class="c-article-equation"><div class="c-article-equation__content"><span class="mathjax-tex">$${T}_{d,j}={T}_{d{\rm{,}}MERRA{\rm{2}}}+{\varepsilon }_{{T}_{d,j}}$$</span></div><div class="c-article-equation__number">
                    (3)
                </div></div><div id="Equ4" class="c-article-equation"><div class="c-article-equation__content"><span class="mathjax-tex">$${SW}_{j}=\left({\rm{1}}-{\gamma }_{j}\right)\cdot {SW}_{MERRA{\rm{2}}}$$</span></div><div class="c-article-equation__number">
                    (4)
                </div></div><p>where <i>PPT</i>, <i>T</i><sub><i>a</i></sub>, <i>T</i><sub><i>d</i></sub>, and <i>SW</i> represent the precipitation, air temperature, dew point temperature, and shortwave radiation forcings respectively, the subscript <i>j</i> represents the perturbed forcing realization within the ensemble and <i>MERRA2</i> represents the downscaled MERRA2 forcings using the downscaling described above. The random variable <i>b</i> represents a lognormally distributed multiplicative precipitation perturbation. The random variable <i>ε</i><sub><i>Ta</i></sub> and <i>ε</i><sub><i>Td</i></sub> represent normally distributed additive error perturbations of air temperature and dew point temperature, respectively. The random variable <i>γ</i> represents a normally distributed multiplicative shortwave perturbation that varies with solar index (<i>SI</i>, ratio of MERRA2 solar radiation over clear sky solar radiation) to account for varying errors under clear-sky vs. cloudy-sky conditions<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 34" title="Margulis, S. A., Liu, Y. & Baldo, E. A Joint Landsat- and MODIS-Based Reanalysis Approach for Midlatitude Montane Seasonal Snow Characterization. Front. Earth Sci. 7, 272 (2019)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR34" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e1549">34</a></sup>.</p><p>The moments of the precipitation parameter <i>b</i> distribution are estimated based on the same methodology described in Liu <i>et al</i>.<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 54" title="Liu, Y. & Margulis, S. A. Deriving Bias and Uncertainty in MERRA-2 Snowfall Precipitation Over High Mountain Asia. Front. Earth Sci. 7, 280 (2019)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR54" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e1562">54</a></sup> from a sub-sample of 10 tiles across the WUS spanning a range of physiography and climatology (Fig. <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="figure anchor" href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#Fig1">1</a> in bold boxes). The precipitation uncertainty is quantified by running the snow reanalysis framework using a uniform (i.e., “uninformative”) distribution for the parameter <i>b</i>~<i>U</i>(0.1, 5) at the 10 tiles. After assimilating fSCA measurements using the PBS approach, a log-normal distribution is fitted to the posterior <i>b</i> values from all pixels and replicates in those 10 tiles (Table <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="table anchor" href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#Tab3">3</a>). The fitted distribution is then treated as the prior distribution for the full WUS–SR domain.</p><div class="c-article-table" data-test="inline-table" data-container-section="table" id="table-4"><figure><figcaption class="c-article-table__figcaption"><b id="Tab3" data-test="table-caption">Table 3 Distributions of meteorological forcings and model parameter perturbations with details described in the Uncertainty Parameters and Measurement Error section.</b></figcaption><div class="u-hide-print"><a class="c-article__pill-button" data-test="table-link" data-track="click" data-track-action="view table" data-track-label="button" rel="nofollow" href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7/tables/4" aria-label="Full size table 4"><span>Full size table</span><svg width="16" height="16" focusable="false" role="img" aria-hidden="true" class="u-icon"><use xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="#icon-eds-i-chevron-right-small"></use></svg></a></div></figure></div><p>The derivation of uncertainty models for air temperature, dew point temperature and shortwave uncertainty analysis followed Girotto <i>et al</i>.<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 53" title="Girotto, M., Margulis, S. A. & Durand, M. Probabilistic SWE reanalysis as a generalization of deterministic SWE reconstruction techniques: PROBABILISTIC SWE REANALYSIS. Hydrol. Process. 28, 3875–3895 (2014)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR53" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e1993">53</a></sup> by comparing downscaled MERRA2 forcings to <i>in situ</i> measurements across the WUS. The uncertainties of MERRA2 forcings are quantified based on <i>in situ</i> Snow Telemetry network (SNOTEL) and Soil Climate Analysis Network (SCAN) air temperature, shortwave, and dew point temperature measurements. For air temperature and dew point temperature, the differences between downscaled MERRA2 and <i>in situ</i> data (i.e., distribution of temperature errors <i>ε</i><sub><i>Ta</i></sub> and <i>ε</i><sub><i>Td</i></sub>) are fitted with normal distributions separately. The <i>in situ</i> solar radiation measurements and downscaled MERRA2 data are used to fit normal distributions (Table <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="table anchor" href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#Tab3">3</a>) to the multiplicative parameter <i>γ</i> whose mean and standard deviation are polynomial functions of the <i>SI</i>.</p><p>Table <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="table anchor" href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#Tab3">3</a> summarizes the fitted parameters of the uncertainty models. The multiplicative precipitation factor <i>b</i> follows a lognormal distribution with mean of 1.80 and coefficient of variation (CV) of 0.69, which corrects the underestimation in raw MERRA2 precipitation used as input to the LSM. The normally distributed air temperature error <i>ε</i><sub><i>Ta</i></sub>, has a positive mean of 0.85 K, while the dew point temperature error <i>ε</i><sub><i>Td</i></sub> has mean of −1.37 K. The quantified mean parameters identify (and correct) a cold and dry bias in the MERRA2 data before running the LSM-SDC to generate prior snow estimates.</p><h4 class="c-article__sub-heading c-article__sub-heading--small" id="Sec8">Perturbed model parameters</h4><p>The snow reanalysis framework additionally acknowledges sub-grid snow heterogeneity (resulting in fractional snow-covered area) and the uncertainties in snow albedo that result from different dust conditions.</p><p>The sub-grid distribution of snow cover and SWE is captured by the Liston<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 39" title="Liston, G. E. Representing Subgrid Snow Cover Heterogeneities in Regional and Global Models. J. Clim. 17, 1381–1397 (2004)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR39" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e2064">39</a></sup> SDC model with the free parameter representing the coefficient of variation (<i>β</i>) of the lognormal distribution. The free parameter <i>β</i> itself is treated as a uniformly distributed (~<i>U</i>(0.05, 0.8)<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 34" title="Margulis, S. A., Liu, Y. & Baldo, E. A Joint Landsat- and MODIS-Based Reanalysis Approach for Midlatitude Montane Seasonal Snow Characterization. Front. Earth Sci. 7, 272 (2019)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR34" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e2077">34</a></sup>) uncertainty parameter.</p><p>The uncertainties in snow albedo in the visible band are accounted for in the BATS snow albedo (<i>α</i><sub><i>vis</i></sub>) model:</p><div id="Equ5" class="c-article-equation"><div class="c-article-equation__content"><span class="mathjax-tex">$${\alpha }_{vis,j}=\left({\rm{1}}-{C}_{vis{\rm{,}}j}{f}_{age}\right)\cdot {\alpha }_{VO}$$</span></div><div class="c-article-equation__number">
                    (5)
                </div></div><p>where <i>C</i><sub><i>vis</i></sub> is a uniformly distributed (~<i>U</i>(0.2, 0.45)<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 34" title="Margulis, S. A., Liu, Y. & Baldo, E. A Joint Landsat- and MODIS-Based Reanalysis Approach for Midlatitude Montane Seasonal Snow Characterization. Front. Earth Sci. 7, 272 (2019)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR34" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e2211">34</a></sup>) uncertainty parameter chosen to span clean to dusty snow conditions (Table <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="table anchor" href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#Tab3">3</a>). The variable <i>f</i><sub><i>age</i></sub> represents the fraction of snow albedo reduction due to snow aging. The fresh snow albedo <i>α</i><sub><i>VO</i></sub> is set to 0.95. Such an approach does not include any explicit information on dust, but instead tries to realistically span the uncertainty when dust may be present.</p><h4 class="c-article__sub-heading c-article__sub-heading--small" id="Sec9">Measurement error</h4><p>The data assimilation framework requires specification of fSCA error standard deviation as an input. The measurement error of retrieved Landsat fSCA is specified as 10% at ~500 m, which is consistent with previous work<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 34" title="Margulis, S. A., Liu, Y. & Baldo, E. A Joint Landsat- and MODIS-Based Reanalysis Approach for Midlatitude Montane Seasonal Snow Characterization. Front. Earth Sci. 7, 272 (2019)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR34" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e2238">34</a>,<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 50" title="Liu, Y., Fang, Y. & Margulis, S. A. Spatiotemporal distribution of seasonal snow water equivalent in High Mountain Asia from an 18-year Landsat–MODIS era snow reanalysis dataset. The Cryosphere 15, 5261–5280 (2021)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR50" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e2241">50</a></sup>. The measurement errors between different fSCA measurements are assumed to be uncorrelated in space and time.</p></div></div></section><section data-title="Data Records"><div class="c-article-section" id="Sec10-section"><h2 class="c-article-section__title js-section-title js-c-reading-companion-sections-item" id="Sec10">Data Records</h2><div class="c-article-section__content" id="Sec10-content"><p>The raw gridded 16 arcsecond (~ 500 m) daily snow reanalysis dataset over the WUS (WUS–SR) is publicly available at the National Snow and Ice Data Center (<a href="https://doi.org/10.5067/PP7T2GBI52I2">https://doi.org/10.5067/PP7T2GBI52I2</a>)<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 27" title="Fang, Y., Liu, Y. & Margulis, S. Western United States UCLA Daily Snow Reanalysis. NASA Earth Data, 
                  https://doi.org/10.5067/PP7T2GBI52I2
                  
                 (2022)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR27" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e2262">27</a></sup> in netCDF format. It starts from WY 1985 (Oct. 1<sup>st</sup>, 1984) to WY 2021 (Sept. 30<sup>th</sup>, 2021) and will be extended for future WYs when available (Table <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="table anchor" href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#Tab4">4</a>). The output files store daily maps of posterior SWE, fSCA, and snow depth within a 1° by 1° tile (Fig. <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="figure anchor" href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#Fig1">1</a>) for a given WY. The results presented in this paper show the ensemble median of SWE (an output that is determined from the discrete PDF of posterior weights). The ensemble mean, standard deviation, and interquartile range of outputs are also provided in the dataset. Ancillary or derived data products (e.g., non-seasonal snow mask) are available upon request.</p><div class="c-article-table" data-test="inline-table" data-container-section="table" id="table-5"><figure><figcaption class="c-article-table__figcaption"><b id="Tab4" data-test="table-caption">Table 4 Spatial and temporal information of the WUS–SR dataset.</b></figcaption><div class="u-hide-print"><a class="c-article__pill-button" data-test="table-link" data-track="click" data-track-action="view table" data-track-label="button" rel="nofollow" href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7/tables/5" aria-label="Full size table 5"><span>Full size table</span><svg width="16" height="16" focusable="false" role="img" aria-hidden="true" class="u-icon"><use xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="#icon-eds-i-chevron-right-small"></use></svg></a></div></figure></div></div></div></section><section data-title="Technical Verification"><div class="c-article-section" id="Sec11-section"><h2 class="c-article-section__title js-section-title js-c-reading-companion-sections-item" id="Sec11">Technical Verification</h2><div class="c-article-section__content" id="Sec11-content"><p>Figure <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="figure anchor" href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#Fig4">4</a> shows a sample of the seasonal cycle and spatial distribution of SWE over HUC2 basins and the entire WUS domain in WY 2019. No SWE or snow depth measurements are assimilated in deriving the WUS–SR dataset. Thus, <i>in situ</i> SWE and snow depth measurements, and ASO SWE and snow depth estimates are used as independent verification datasets. Landsat fSCA measurements are assimilated into the snow reanalysis framework assuming a measurement error (standard deviation) of 10%<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 34" title="Margulis, S. A., Liu, Y. & Baldo, E. A Joint Landsat- and MODIS-Based Reanalysis Approach for Midlatitude Montane Seasonal Snow Characterization. Front. Earth Sci. 7, 272 (2019)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR34" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e2424">34</a></sup>. Though Landsat fSCA cannot be used for independent verification, the WUS–SR posterior fSCA estimates, which are fitted to these measurements using a likelihood function, are expected to have comparable bulk error. The snow reanalysis framework has been successfully applied previously to generate datasets over the Sierra Nevada, Andes, and High Mountain Asia<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 33" title="Margulis, S. A., Cortés, G., Girotto, M. & Durand, M. A Landsat-Era Sierra Nevada Snow Reanalysis (1985–2015). J. Hydrometeorol. 17, 1203–1221 (2016)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR33" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e2428">33</a>,<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 50" title="Liu, Y., Fang, Y. & Margulis, S. A. Spatiotemporal distribution of seasonal snow water equivalent in High Mountain Asia from an 18-year Landsat–MODIS era snow reanalysis dataset. The Cryosphere 15, 5261–5280 (2021)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR50" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e2431">50</a>,<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 52" title="Cortés, G. & Margulis, S. Impacts of El Niño and La Niña on interannual snow accumulation in the Andes: Results from a high-resolution 31 year reanalysis. Geophys. Res. Lett. 44, 6859–6867 (2017)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR52" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e2434">52</a></sup>.</p><div class="c-article-section__figure js-c-reading-companion-figures-item" data-test="figure" data-container-section="figure" id="figure-4" data-title="Fig. 4"><figure><figcaption><b id="Fig4" class="c-article-section__figure-caption" data-test="figure-caption-text">Fig. 4</b></figcaption><div class="c-article-section__figure-content"><div class="c-article-section__figure-item"><picture class="c-article-section__figure-picture"><source type="image/webp" srcset="//media.springernature.com/lw685/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41597-022-01768-7/MediaObjects/41597_2022_1768_Fig4_HTML.png?as=webp"><img aria-describedby="figure-4-desc" src="//media.springernature.com/lw685/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41597-022-01768-7/MediaObjects/41597_2022_1768_Fig4_HTML.png" alt="Fig. 4" loading="lazy" width="685" height="353"></picture><div class="c-article-section__figure-link"><a class="c-article__pill-button" data-test="article-link" data-track="click" data-track-label="button" data-track-action="view figure" href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7/figures/4" data-track-dest="link:Figure4 Full size image" aria-label="Full size image figure 4" rel="nofollow"><span>Full size image</span><svg width="16" height="16" focusable="false" role="img" aria-hidden="true" class="u-icon"><use xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="#icon-eds-i-chevron-right-small"></use></svg></a></div></div><div class="c-article-section__figure-description" data-test="bottom-caption" id="figure-4-desc"><p>Illustrative results from the WUS–SR SWE estimates in WY 2019. (<b>a</b>) Seasonal cycle of SWE volume (km<sup>3</sup>) integrated over HUC2 basins. (<b>b</b>) Spatial distribution of SWE (meters) over part of the Sierra Nevada on March 1<sup>st</sup>, WY 2019. (<b>c</b>) Spatial distribution of WUS SWE (meters) on March 1<sup>st</sup>, 2019. The boxed area in (<b>c</b>) represents that shown in (<b>b</b>).</p></div></div></figure></div><h3 class="c-article__sub-heading" id="Sec12">Verification with <i>in situ</i> data</h3><p>In this section, grid-averaged reanalysis SWE and snow depth are compared with point-scale <i>in situ</i> measurements. It should be acknowledged a priori that there are inevitable representativeness issues in the comparison between point-scale <i>in situ</i> data and grid-averaged snow reanalysis data. The WUS–SR estimates are modeled with assumed sub-grid heterogeneity within each ~500 m grid cell (which is modeled via a lognormal distribution) meant to account for the complex sub-grid variations in terrain (elevation, slope, aspect), forest cover, and meteorological forcings. Given that <i>in situ</i> stations are often sited in non-representative regions of a grid cell (i.e., in sheltered flat forest clearings), it is unlikely that the grid-averaged SWE/snow depth (spanning ~ 250,000 m<sup>2</sup>) should match the point-scale <i>in situ</i> SWE/snow depth (spanning ~10 m<sup>2</sup>). Nevertheless, <i>in situ</i> measurements, from the SNOTEL and CA Department of Water Resources (CADWR) networks, represent the best available data that covers much of the WUS and extends back several decades. While not expected to match each other, the verification herein is meant to illustrate consistency between the <i>in situ</i> measurements and WUS–SR estimates.</p><h4 class="c-article__sub-heading c-article__sub-heading--small" id="Sec13">Peak SWE comparison with in situ data</h4><p><i>In situ</i> SWE measurements from WY 1985 to 2021 are taken from 1) the SNOTEL network (<a href="https://www.wcc.nrcs.usda.gov/snow/">https://www.wcc.nrcs.usda.gov/snow/</a>) managed by the U.S. Natural Resources Conservation Service (NRCS), and 2) CADWR (<a href="https://cdec.water.ca.gov/dynamicapp/staSearch">https://cdec.water.ca.gov/dynamicapp/staSearch</a> from sensor type: “SNO ADJ (82)”), collections of automated snow pillows in the WUS. For <i>in situ</i> verification, we pair each <i>in situ</i> site with the closest snow reanalysis grid based on the geolocation of these two datasets. The precision of <i>in situ</i> coordinate values varies from 0.000001° (<1 m) to 0.01° (>1 km). Considering the potential for geolocation mismatch, the nine nearest pixels<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 32" title="Margulis, S. A., Girotto, M., Cortés, G. & Durand, M. A Particle Batch Smoother Approach to Snow Water Equivalent Estimation. J. Hydrometeorol. 16, 1752–1772 (2015)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR32" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e2545">32</a>,<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 33" title="Margulis, S. A., Cortés, G., Girotto, M. & Durand, M. A Landsat-Era Sierra Nevada Snow Reanalysis (1985–2015). J. Hydrometeorol. 17, 1203–1221 (2016)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR33" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e2548">33</a>,<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 55" title="Girotto, M., Cortés, G., Margulis, S. A. & Durand, M. Examining spatial and temporal variability in snow water equivalent using a 27 year reanalysis: Kern River watershed, Sierra Nevada. Water Resour. Res. 50, 6713–6734 (2014)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR55" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e2551">55</a></sup> are additionally used to compare <i>in situ</i> and WUS–SR peak SWE. In this latter approach, the differences between <i>in situ</i> peak SWE and the neighboring WUS–SR grid cell peak SWE with the smallest difference among the nine nearest snow reanalysis grids are used. To compare the SWE on the same day, peak SWE day determined by <i>in situ</i> SWE is used to extract peak SWE from both datasets throughout the paper.</p><p>Figure <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="figure anchor" href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#Fig5">5</a> presents the density scatter plots comparing <i>in situ</i> peak SWE values against collocated grid-cell posterior peak SWE values. Peak SWE values less than 1 cm are screened out from the comparison. In total, 928 <i>in situ</i> sites are used in the comparison with the WUS–SR SWE estimates. To understand the performance of the WUS–SR dataset across different regimes in the WUS, verification is conducted for each HUC2 basin. The comparison is quantified using correlation coefficient (<i>R</i>), mean difference (<i>MD</i>), and root mean square difference (<i>RMSD</i>). Table <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="table anchor" href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#Tab5">5</a> summarizes the number of total site-years, and statistics for both prior and posterior reanalysis SWE against <i>in situ</i> SWE within each HUC2 basin and over the WUS.</p><div class="c-article-section__figure js-c-reading-companion-figures-item" data-test="figure" data-container-section="figure" id="figure-5" data-title="Fig. 5"><figure><figcaption><b id="Fig5" class="c-article-section__figure-caption" data-test="figure-caption-text">Fig. 5</b></figcaption><div class="c-article-section__figure-content"><div class="c-article-section__figure-item"><picture class="c-article-section__figure-picture"><source type="image/webp" srcset="//media.springernature.com/lw685/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41597-022-01768-7/MediaObjects/41597_2022_1768_Fig5_HTML.png?as=webp"><img aria-describedby="figure-5-desc" src="//media.springernature.com/lw685/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41597-022-01768-7/MediaObjects/41597_2022_1768_Fig5_HTML.png" alt="Fig. 5" loading="lazy" width="685" height="478"></picture><div class="c-article-section__figure-link"><a class="c-article__pill-button" data-test="article-link" data-track="click" data-track-label="button" data-track-action="view figure" href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7/figures/5" data-track-dest="link:Figure5 Full size image" aria-label="Full size image figure 5" rel="nofollow"><span>Full size image</span><svg width="16" height="16" focusable="false" role="img" aria-hidden="true" class="u-icon"><use xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="#icon-eds-i-chevron-right-small"></use></svg></a></div></div><div class="c-article-section__figure-description" data-test="bottom-caption" id="figure-5-desc"><p>Density scatter plot of <i>in situ</i> (snow pillow) peak SWE and collocated posterior (grid-average) peak SWE grouped by HUC2 basins over WYs 1985 to 2021. The solid black line is the 1:1 line. The correlation coefficient (<i>R</i>), mean difference (<i>MD</i>), and root mean square difference (<i>RMSD</i>) are shown for each HUC2 basin. <i>In situ</i> data with peak SWE values greater than 1 cm are included in the comparison.</p></div></div></figure></div><div class="c-article-table" data-test="inline-table" data-container-section="table" id="table-6"><figure><figcaption class="c-article-table__figcaption"><b id="Tab5" data-test="table-caption">Table 5 Number of <i>in situ</i> sites and comparison metrics between <i>in situ</i> (snow pillow) peak SWE and collocated grid-averaged snow reanalysis prior and posterior (post.) peak SWE grouped by HUC2 basins.</b></figcaption><div class="u-hide-print"><a class="c-article__pill-button" data-test="table-link" data-track="click" data-track-action="view table" data-track-label="button" rel="nofollow" href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7/tables/6" aria-label="Full size table 6"><span>Full size table</span><svg width="16" height="16" focusable="false" role="img" aria-hidden="true" class="u-icon"><use xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="#icon-eds-i-chevron-right-small"></use></svg></a></div></figure></div><p>Compared with the performance of the prior peak SWE estimates (i.e., not constrained by Landsat fSCA), posterior SWE estimates show a better correlation (higher <i>R</i>) with less bias and random error (lower <i>MD</i> and <i>RMSD</i>) than the prior SWE over most of the HUC2 basins. Posterior SWE in CA has the highest correlation against <i>in situ</i> SWE (<i>R = </i>0.82). The correlations with <i>in situ</i> SWE over the entire WUS are improved from 0.74 (prior) to 0.77 (posterior). Posterior peak SWE in UCRB has lower bias and uncertainty compared against <i>in situ</i> data with a relatively small <i>MD</i> of 0.06 m in absolute value (reduced by 62% from prior <i>MD</i>) and <i>RMSD</i> of 0.19 m (reduced by 27%). Over the WUS, <i>in situ</i> peak SWE is (on average) larger than the WUS–SR peak SWE (negative <i>MD</i>). Sub-grid topographic variability, snow-forest interactions, and wind-driven snow redistribution may all cause differences seen between grid-averaged peak SWE and point-scale <i>in situ</i> peak SWE. The statistics for PN indicate comparable correlation of <i>in situ</i> and both prior and posterior snow reanalysis, however the <i>MD</i> and <i>RMSD</i> do not get improved from posterior to prior. Fewer cloud-free fSCA measurements are available in PN, which limits the improvement of snow reanalysis SWE via data assimilation.</p><p>To acknowledge the potential geolocation mismatch, Fig. <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="figure anchor" href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#Fig6">6</a> provides verification of <i>in situ</i> peak SWE and posterior reanalysis peak SWE using an approach comparing to the best match among the nine nearest pixels. The WUS-wide correlation coefficient (<i>R</i>), <i>MD</i> and <i>RMSD</i> of posterior peak SWE and <i>in situ</i> peak SWE is 0.91, −0.08 m, 0.18 m, respectively. Compared to the approach used in Fig. <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="figure anchor" href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#Fig5">5</a>, the posterior reanalysis peak SWE in Fig. <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="figure anchor" href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#Fig6">6</a> (as expected) is more correlated with <i>in situ</i> peak SWE (<i>R</i> values above 0.9), and has lower <i>MD</i> (<0.13 m) and <i>RMSD</i> (<0.24 m) over the WUS and at all HUC2 basins. Posterior reanalysis peak SWE is still lower than the <i>in situ</i> peak SWE at most of the sites, with the largest <i>MD</i> found in the PN. The PN has fewer cloud-free fSCA measurements, which may lead to larger errors than in regions with fewer cloud-contaminated images. The <i>MD</i> in CA is −0.07 m, which is within the range of −0.12 to 0.01 m as reported in Margulis <i>et al</i>.<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 33" title="Margulis, S.
