Hydrometeorol. 17, 1203–1221 (2016)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR33" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e3226">33</a></sup>, where the original 90-m Sierra Nevada SWE reanalysis was compared against <i>in situ</i> peak SWE using the same approach.</p><div class="c-article-section__figure js-c-reading-companion-figures-item" data-test="figure" data-container-section="figure" id="figure-6" The median <i>RMSD</i> remains stable at ~ 0.18 m for forest fractions below 40%, and gradually increases to ~ 0.38 m when forest fraction increases to over 60%. The larger <i>RMSD</i> at higher forest fraction pixels might be caused by 1) larger disparities between <i>in situ</i> sites (that tend to be in forest clearings) and collocated pixels with large averaged forest coverage fraction and/or 2) larger estimation errors in WUS–SR peak SWE in areas with large forest coverage. Aside from forest coverage effects, the difference between <i>in situ</i> and posterior peak SWE is impacted by the number of fSCA measurements as illustrated in Fig. <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="figure anchor" href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#Fig7">7b</a>. When over 40 fSCA measurements (after cloud screening) are available, the median of absolute difference is as low as ~ 0.11 m. As the number of annual fSCA measurements is reduced, the median and spread of the absolute difference of peak SWE for each year increased. Figure <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="figure anchor" href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#Fig7">7c</a> show that the peak SWE days determined by <i>in situ</i> data is highly correlated to peak SWE days determined by posterior WUS–SR SWE (<i>R</i> = 0.73). Overall, <i>in situ</i> SWE peaks later than the WUS–SR SWE with a <i>MD</i> value of −10 days.</p><div class="c-article-section__figure js-c-reading-companion-figures-item" data-test="figure" data-container-section="figure" id="figure-7" data-title="Fig. 7"><figure><figcaption><b id="Fig7" class="c-article-section__figure-caption" data-test="figure-caption-text">Fig. 7</b></figcaption><div class="c-article-section__figure-content"><div class="c-article-section__figure-item"><picture class="c-article-section__figure-picture"><source type="image/webp" srcset="//media.springernature.com/lw685/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41597-022-01768-7/MediaObjects/41597_2022_1768_Fig7_HTML.png?as=webp"><img aria-describedby="figure-7-desc" src="//media.springernature.com/lw685/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41597-022-01768-7/MediaObjects/41597_2022_1768_Fig7_HTML.png" alt="Fig. 7" loading="lazy" width="685" height="248"></picture><div class="c-article-section__figure-link"><a class="c-article__pill-button" data-test="article-link" data-track="click" data-track-label="button" data-track-action="view figure" href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7/figures/7" data-track-dest="link:Figure7 Full size image" aria-label="Full size image figure 7" rel="nofollow"><span>Full size image</span><svg width="16" height="16" focusable="false" role="img" aria-hidden="true" class="u-icon"><use xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="#icon-eds-i-chevron-right-small"></use></svg></a></div></div><div class="c-article-section__figure-description" data-test="bottom-caption" id="figure-7-desc"><p>(<b>a</b>) <i>RMSD</i> of peak SWE as a function of averaged forest fraction for each site. <i>RMSD</i> is determined at each site from the 37-year peak SWE from <i>in situ</i> and posterior WUS–SR. Daily SWE values less than 2.54 mm are excluded.</p></div></div></figure></div><p>Over the entire WUS, posterior daily SWE at <i>in situ</i> sites have high correlations (median of 0.79), small <i>MD</i> (median of −0.08 m) and <i>RMSD</i> (median of 0.17 m) against <i>in situ</i> SWE. The comparison suggests that posterior daily SWE agrees reasonably well with daily <i>in situ</i> SWE, especially in CA and UCRB with higher correlations and relatively lower <i>MD</i> and <i>RMSD</i>. Daily posterior SWE is slightly lower than point-scale <i>in situ</i> SWE (Fig. <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="figure anchor" href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#Fig6">6b</a>. negative <i>MD</i> in blue) at most of the sites. At some <i>in situ</i> sites in the western PN, posterior SWE shows higher differences. Figure <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="figure anchor" href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#Fig8">8(e,f)</a> show that low <i>MD</i> and <i>RMSD</i> expressed as percent of peak SWE are observed at some sites with high <i>MD</i> and <i>RMSD</i> due to deep snow. For sites with both large absolute and percent of differences, some of these differences may represent larger errors caused by fewer available fSCA measurements after clouds screening. Finer resolutions may be needed to capture large sub-grid SWE values.</p><h4 class="c-article__sub-heading c-article__sub-heading--small" id="Sec15">Peak snow depth comparison with in situ data</h4><p><i>In situ</i> snow depth measurements are taken from the same sources as SWE (i.e., NRCS and CADWR from sensor type: “SNOW DP (18)”). Similar verification steps as with peak SWE (Fig. <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="figure anchor" href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#Fig5">5</a>) are conducted for snow depth as shown in Fig. <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="figure anchor" href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#Fig9">9</a>. Compared to the SWE measurements, however, <i>in situ</i> snow depth measurements appear to be of lower quality with some station-years showing snow depth with persistently high values throughout the year, non-physical oscillations in the measurements, and other erroneous behavior that are clearly inconsistent with the corresponding SWE measurements. Hence, extra screening is applied to the data before being used for verification. <i>In situ</i> snow depth measurements that changed by more than 1 m in a single day were assumed erroneous and excluded from the analysis. Further, assuming snow density is within the range of 200 to 500 kg/m<sup>3</sup> at the peak day, snow depth measurements outside 2–5 times the corresponding SWE measurements were removed. To avoid incorrectly diagnosing peak snow depth day from snow depth measurements with missing data after screening, the <i>in situ</i> peak SWE day was used to determine the <i>in situ</i> snow depth used for comparison with posterior reanalysis estimates. Overall, posterior peak snow depth is correlated with <i>in situ</i> peak snow depth (<i>R</i> = 0.72) and has an <i>MD</i> of −0.36 m and <i>RMSD</i> of 0.66 m over the WUS. Compared to the results from peak SWE verification, the correlation coefficient between <i>in situ</i> and posterior peak snow depth is about the same at all HUC2 basins, with the highest value (<i>R</i> = 0.81) in CA. The <i>MD</i> and <i>RMSD</i> values for peak snow depth are around 2 to 3 times larger than those in peak SWE, partially caused by larger snow depth values than SWE and perhaps the poorer quality of <i>in situ</i> snow depth measurements.</p><div class="c-article-section__figure js-c-reading-companion-figures-item" data-test="figure" data-container-section="figure" id="figure-9" data-title="Fig. 9"><figure><figcaption><b id="Fig9" class="c-article-section__figure-caption" data-test="figure-caption-text">Fig. 9</b></figcaption><div class="c-article-section__figure-content"><div class="c-article-section__figure-item"><picture class="c-article-section__figure-picture"><source type="image/webp" srcset="//media.springernature.com/lw685/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41597-022-01768-7/MediaObjects/41597_2022_1768_Fig9_HTML.png?as=webp"><img aria-describedby="figure-9-desc" src="//media.springernature.com/lw685/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41597-022-01768-7/MediaObjects/41597_2022_1768_Fig9_HTML.png" alt="Fig. 9" loading="lazy" width="685" height="488"></picture><div class="c-article-section__figure-link"><a class="c-article__pill-button" data-test="article-link" data-track="click" data-track-label="button" data-track-action="view figure" href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7/figures/9" data-track-dest="link:Figure9 Full size image" aria-label="Full size image figure 9" rel="nofollow"><span>Full size image</span><svg width="16" height="16" focusable="false" role="img" aria-hidden="true" class="u-icon"><use xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="#icon-eds-i-chevron-right-small"></use></svg></a></div></div><div class="c-article-section__figure-description" data-test="bottom-caption" id="figure-9-desc"><p>Same as Fig. <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="figure anchor" href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#Fig5">5</a> but for peak snow depth. Peak day is determined by <i>in situ</i> peak SWE. <i>In situ</i> data with peak snow depth values greater than 5 cm are included in the comparison.</p></div></div></figure></div><h3 class="c-article__sub-heading" id="Sec16">Verification with airborne snow observatory (ASO) data</h3><p>The WUS–SR estimates are further verified against gridded SWE and snow depth estimates from ASO<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 11" title="Painter, T. H. et al. The Airborne Snow Observatory: Fusion of scanning lidar, imaging spectrometer, and physically-based modeling for mapping snow water equivalent and snow albedo. Remote Sens. Environ. 184, 139–152 (2016)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR11" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e3564">11</a>,<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" title="Painter, T. ASO L4 Lidar Snow Water Equivalent 50m UTM Grid, Version 1. NASA National Snow and Ice Data Center DAAC 
                  https://doi.org/10.5067/M4TUH28NHL4Z
                  
                 (2018)." href="#ref-CR56" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e3567">56</a>,<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" title="Painter, T. ASO L4 Lidar Snow Depth 50m UTM Grid, Version 1. NASA National Snow and Ice Data Center DAAC 
                  https://doi.org/10.5067/STOT5I0U1WVI
                  
                 (2018)." href="#ref-CR57" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e3567_1">57</a>,<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 58" title="Airborne Snow Observatories, Inc. 
                  https://data.airbornesnowobservatories.com/
                  
                 (2020)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR58" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e3570">58</a></sup>. The lidar-based ASO measures snow depth via an airborne laser scanner (ALS) based on the differences in elevations between a snow-off day and snow-on days. ASO SWE is estimated from the high-resolution snow depth measurements and modeled snow density<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 11" title="Painter, T. H. et al. The Airborne Snow Observatory: Fusion of scanning lidar, imaging spectrometer, and physically-based modeling for mapping snow water equivalent and snow albedo. Remote Sens. Environ. 184, 139–152 (2016)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR11" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e3574">11</a></sup>. For comparison, the 50-m ASO SWE and snow depth snapshots are aggregated to the WUS–SR SWE model resolution. ASO data is available over select sites in California, Colorado, and Washington starting from 2013. While abundant snapshots are available in the Tuolumne River Basin in California, limited snapshots (commonly once per year) were taken at most of the ASO sites. ASO snow depth is a relatively accurate measurement with measurement error less than 0.02 m at a 50 m × 50 m grid. Model error (5%–8%<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 11" title="Painter, T. H. et al. The Airborne Snow Observatory: Fusion of scanning lidar, imaging spectrometer, and physically-based modeling for mapping snow water equivalent and snow albedo. Remote Sens. Environ. 184, 139–152 (2016)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR11" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e3578">11</a></sup>) could exist in modeled snow density, which is expected to propagate to ASO SWE estimates.</p><p>ASO SWE and snow depth estimates are compared with prior and posterior ensemble median SWE and snow depth maps on coincident days (Figs. <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="figure anchor" href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#Fig10">10</a> and <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="figure anchor" href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#Fig11">11</a>). Tables <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="table anchor" href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#Tab6">6</a> and <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="table anchor" href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#Tab7">7</a> reports the statistical metrics for comparisons closest to April 1<sup>st</sup> at sampled ASO basins: USCATB (Tuolumne River Basin, California), USWAOL (Olympic Mountains, Washington), and USCOCM (Aspen/Castle-Maroon, Colorado).</p><h4 class="c-article__sub-heading c-article__sub-heading--small" id="Sec17">SWE map comparison</h4><p>For the California domain (USCATB, Fig. <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="figure anchor" href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#Fig10">10</a> left column, Table <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="table anchor" href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#Tab6">6</a>), posterior SWE is highly correlated with ASO SWE (ranging from 0.81 to 0.91) compared against prior SWE (ranging from 0.50 to 0.71). A negative <i>MD</i> indicates that the WUS–SR SWE is less than ASO SWE (on average) in Tuolumne. The difference significantly decreases from prior to posterior estimates in most years, along with decreased <i>RMSD</i>. WY 2015 was a historically dry year, in which posterior SWE shows no bias compared with ASO SWE, with a small <i>RMSD</i> of 0.07 m. Posterior SWE in WY 2017 has the highest correlation (0.91) with ASO SWE compared with a lower correlation (0.56) in prior SWE. <i>MD</i> drops from −0.13 m to −0.04 m, and <i>RMSD</i> decreases by half from prior to posterior in WY 2017. Figure <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="figure anchor" href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#Fig10">10</a> (left column) illustrates that Tuolumne-averaged posterior SWE (1.23 m) is comparable with ASO SWE (1.27 m), suggesting that the posterior WUS–SR SWE and ASO are in good agreement with respect to the basin-wide mean SWE. The prior underestimates SWE at high elevations in the northern parts and southern edges of Tuolumne basins whereas it overestimates shallow SWE near the basin outlet. The performance of the spatially distributed posterior SWE is considerably improved over the prior compared with ASO SWE. Though <i>MD</i> in WY 2019 increases from −0.06 m to −0.14 m (from prior to posterior), <i>RMSD</i> in that year decreases from 0.34 m to 0.27 m. The differences between prior SWE and ASO SWE are large in absolute values, while large positive differences are offset by negative differences causing a low <i>MD</i> for prior SWE in WY 2019.</p><div class="c-article-section__figure js-c-reading-companion-figures-item" data-test="figure" data-container-section="figure" id="figure-10" data-title="Fig. 10"><figure><figcaption><b id="Fig10" class="c-article-section__figure-caption" data-test="figure-caption-text">Fig. 10</b></figcaption><div class="c-article-section__figure-content"><div class="c-article-section__figure-item"><picture class="c-article-section__figure-picture"><source type="image/webp" srcset="//media.springernature.com/lw685/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41597-022-01768-7/MediaObjects/41597_2022_1768_Fig10_HTML.png?as=webp"><img aria-describedby="figure-10-desc" src="//media.springernature.com/lw685/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41597-022-01768-7/MediaObjects/41597_2022_1768_Fig10_HTML.png" alt="Fig. 10" loading="lazy" width="685" height="782"></picture><div class="c-article-section__figure-link"><a class="c-article__pill-button" data-test="article-link" data-track="click" data-track-label="button" data-track-action="view figure" href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7/figures/10" data-track-dest="link:Figure10 Full size image" aria-label="Full size image figure 10" rel="nofollow"><span>Full size image</span><svg width="16" height="16" focusable="false" role="img" aria-hidden="true" class="u-icon"><use xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="#icon-eds-i-chevron-right-small"></use></svg></a></div></div><div class="c-article-section__figure-description" data-test="bottom-caption" id="figure-10-desc"><p>Comparison of ASO SWE with prior and posterior SWE at three ASO sites (top four rows): Tuolumne River Basin, California, (USCATB) in WY 2017 (left column); Olympic Mountains, Washington, (USWAOL) in WY 2016 (middle column); Aspen/Castle-Maroon, Colorado (USCOCM) in WY 2019 (right column). The prior maps are not shown, but instead included implicitly via the difference maps. The bottom row shows the relative <i>RMSD</i> between ASO and WUS–SR SWE as a function of forest fraction. <i>RMSD</i> (from pixels with both ASO and WUS–SR SWE greater than 1 cm) is computed for each forest fraction bin and then normalized by bin-averaged ASO SWE to get relative <i>RMSD</i>.</p></div></div></figure></div><div class="c-article-table" data-test="inline-table" data-container-section="table" id="table-7"><figure><figcaption class="c-article-table__figcaption"><b id="Tab6" data-test="table-caption">Table 6 SWE comparison statistics between ASO SWE estimates and prior and posterior (post.) snow reanalysis SWE on ASO measurement days (Day of Water Year; DOWY) closest to April 1<sup>st</sup>.</b></figcaption><div class="u-hide-print"><a class="c-article__pill-button" data-test="table-link" data-track="click" data-track-action="view table" data-track-label="button" rel="nofollow" href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7/tables/7" aria-label="Full size table 7"><span>Full size table</span><svg width="16" height="16" focusable="false" role="img" aria-hidden="true" class="u-icon"><use xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="#icon-eds-i-chevron-right-small"></use></svg></a></div></figure></div><p>Non-seasonal SWE in portions of the PN (USWAOL) site is a potential error source in both ASO SWE and WUS–SR SWE. Snow depth retrieved from ASO may be erroneous at glacier pixels due to the lack of snow-off flights. The snow reanalysis framework does not include explicit modeling of glaciers. Therefore, non-seasonal snow pixels are removed when comparing the ASO SWE with WUS–SR SWE. This paper generates the WUS–SR non-seasonal snow mask following the method described in Liu <i>et al</i>.<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 50" title="Liu, Y., Fang, Y. & Margulis, S. A. Spatiotemporal distribution of seasonal snow water equivalent in High Mountain Asia from an 18-year Landsat–MODIS era snow reanalysis dataset. The Cryosphere 15, 5261–5280 (2021)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR50" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e4210">50</a></sup>. To summarize the method herein, a pixel is considered as a non-seasonal snow pixel if the annual minimum SWE exceeds 10% of the annual maximum SWE at least once over the dataset period. After applying the non-seasonal snow mask, the mean posterior SWE is 0.51 m which is slightly lower than 0.55 m in ASO SWE. Though the correlation coefficient is high (over 0.8) between prior snow reanalysis SWE and ASO SWE, the <i>MD</i> and <i>RMSD</i> in absolute value is over 0.50 m and 0.60 m respectively, which are both reduced significantly (by 94% and 44% respectively) in the posterior.</p><p>In Colorado (USCOCM), the mean of posterior SWE (0.55 m) is comparable with ASO SWE (0.54 m). The <i>MD</i> is reduced by 98% (to 0.01 m) and <i>RMSD</i> is reduced by 64% (to 0.17 m) from prior to posterior estimates. Although the posterior correlation coefficient is significantly improved over the prior, it is lower than the values seen at the USCATB and USWAOL sites. In Colorado, snow albedo has been shown to be affected by dust, black carbon, and other light-absorbing particles in recent decades<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 59" title="Deems, J. S., Painter, T. H., Barsugli, J. J., Belnap, J. & Udall, B. Combined impacts of current and future dust deposition and regional warming on Colorado River Basin snow dynamics and hydrology. Hydrol. Earth Syst. Sci. 17, 4401–4413 (2013)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR59" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e4229">59</a></sup>. In the current snow reanalysis framework, the impact of dust on snow albedo is modeled through an unconstrained uncertainty parameter. Future work could be done to apply a more explicit treatment of dust impacts on snow albedo to yield potentially improved results.</p><p>The effect of forest fraction on the performance of reanalysis SWE estimates is further illustrated using ASO SWE in Fig. <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="figure anchor" href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#Fig10">10</a>. The Olympics basin has denser forest fraction with a mean of 58%, while the Tuolumne and Aspen/Castle-Maroon basins have mean forest fractions of 17% and 20%, respectively. At all three ASO basins, the relative RMSD of posterior SWE increases with the forest fraction. This is expected since Landsat-derived fSCA is only available over bare areas and/or forest gaps within a pixel. As forest cover increases, less useful information is available, while information is maximized at 0% of forest cover. However, the improvement in prior to posterior SWE estimates increases with forest coverage. This is likely related to the increased complexity of modeling SWE in dense forest areas where the larger uncertainty in forest areas is still reduced with the assimilation of fSCA.</p><h4 class="c-article__sub-heading c-article__sub-heading--small" id="Sec18">Snow depth map comparison</h4><p>Similar to the SWE comparison, posterior snow depth is verified against the ASO snow depth measurements (Fig. <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="figure anchor" href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#Fig11">11</a>, Table <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="table anchor" href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#Tab7">7</a>). The spatial distribution of snow depth differences is comparable to the SWE differences with a correlation coefficient (<i>R</i>) of 0.85 and 0.76 in Washington and Colorado, respectively, and a value above 0.82 in California. In California, the <i>MD</i> of posterior snow depth is reduced by over 30% and <i>RMSD</i> is reduced by over 20% compared to the statistics of prior snow depth over WY 2015 to 2018, and WY 2021. In WY 2019 and 2020, while the posterior <i>MD</i> values are larger than the prior <i>MD</i> (positive and negative differences cancel each other out), the <i>R</i> values are as high as 0.9, and the <i>RMSD</i> values are reduced by 28% and 30%, respectively. In Washington, the posterior <i>MD</i> is close to 0 with <i>RMSD</i> significantly reduced by over 50% from the prior to the posterior estimates. In Colorado, despite the absolute values of <i>MD</i> and <i>RMSD</i> for posterior snow depth being more than twice the values of posterior SWE statistics (due to the larger dynamic range), the estimation of posterior snow depth is significantly improved from the prior snow depth with <i>MD</i> and <i>RMSD</i> reduced by 60% and 40%, respectively.</p><div class="c-article-section__figure class="c-article-section__title js-section-title js-c-reading-companion-sections-item" id="Sec19">Usage Notes</h2><div class="c-article-section__content" id="Sec19-content"><p>The snow reanalysis framework described herein is designed to capture seasonal snow in mountainous areas and does not model glacier processes. However, some non-seasonal snow and glaciers may exist in some regions of the WUS (e.g., the Olympics). Such grid cells can be diagnosed and excluded as described above using the non-seasonal snow mask (as diagnosed via the snow reanalysis framework). It is recommended to mask out these pixels before comparing with other datasets for seasonal snow.</p><p>The WUS–SR dataset is developed from a LSM-SDC model integrated with fSCA data assimilation. The strength of the product is in its space-time continuity where highly uncertain model-based prior estimates are constrained by snow measurements. While uncertainty and bias correction are embedded in the framework, errors and uncertainty in MERRA2 forcings, model parameters, and Landsat fSCA retrievals undoubtedly affect the accuracy of SWE estimates. Developing the uncertainty models using sparse <i>in situ</i> data and application of uncertainty model parameters uniformly over space, likely both oversimplify the true uncertainty and how it varies across different physiographic and climatological gradients.</p><p>Compared with the previous framework and inputs used in the published 90-m reanalysis dataset over the Sierra Nevada<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 33" title="Margulis, S. A., Cortés, G., Girotto, M. & Durand, M. A Landsat-Era Sierra Nevada Snow Reanalysis (1985–2015). J. Hydrometeorol. 17, 1203–1221 (2016)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR33" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e4872">33</a></sup>, some key updates/changes in the current snow reanalysis framework include: (1) use of MERRA2 forcings instead of NLDAS2 forcings, which are globally available and were found to yield marginally better SWE estimates relative to ASO estimates in Tuolumne<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 34" title="Margulis, S. A., Liu, Y. & Baldo, E. A Joint Landsat- and MODIS-Based Reanalysis Approach for Midlatitude Montane Seasonal Snow Characterization. Front. Earth Sci. 7, 272 (2019)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR34" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e4876">34</a></sup>; (2) use of the SRTM DEM (with the ASTER DEM used for void filling) and (3) use of the globally available AVHRR landcover map instead of the National Land Cover Database limited in the U.S. These changes are primarily made to use globally available data for extension and application to broad spatial domains.</p><p>Future versions of this dataset could include: (1) use of multi-source fSCA measurements from Landsat, MODIS, Sentinel, and/or other sources (e.g., VIIRS) to increase the number of cloud-free fSCA images (especially in the Pacific Northwest); (2) examination of the impact of different forcings (e.g., NLDAS2, MERRA2, ERA5) and their uncertainties; (3) use of time-varying forest cover to better reflect transient changes; (4) use of dust-on-snow measurements<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 60" title="Skiles, S. M. et al. Regional variability in dust-on-snow processes and impacts in the Upper Colorado River Basin. Hydrol. Process. 29, 5397–5413 (2015)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR60" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e4883">60</a></sup> to better constrain albedo; and (5) use of multi-resolution approaches<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 61" title="Baldo, E. & Margulis, S. A. Assessment of a multiresolution snow reanalysis framework: a multidecadal reanalysis case over the upper Yampa River basin, Colorado. Hydrol. Earth Syst. Sci. 22, 3575–3587 (2018)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR61" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e4887">61</a>,<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 62" title="Baldo, E. & Margulis, S. A. Implementation of a physiographic complexity-based multiresolution snow modeling scheme: MULTIRESOLUTION SNOW MODELING. Water Resour. Res. 53, 3680–3694 (2017)." href="/articles/s41597-022-01768-7#ref-CR62" id="ref-link-section-d18267266e4890">62</a></sup> to better capture snow estimates in complex terrain with higher resolution where necessary; (6) use of fSCA from Landsat 9 in the future versions.</p></div></div></section>
